section_titles: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
periods.activity_title: Hopping Along — Skip Counting on Number Lines

tasks_in_class.description: Frog jumps 3 steps at a time. Which numbers will the frog touch? Will it touch 67?
Squirrel jumps 4 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? How many jumps to reach 60?
Rabbit jumps 6 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? What is the smallest 3-digit number it lands on? How many jumps?

time_bands.activity: Open by counting aloud together in 3s: 3, 6, 9, 12 … up to 30. Students tap desks on each number spoken, building the physical feel of equal steps before the pictorial number line.

Animal Jumps Q1, p.128 ("Frog jumps 3 steps at a time. Which numbers will the frog touch? Will it touch 67?") — Students fill the hop-ovals on the number line individually, then pair-share the question about 67, articulating why 67 is or is not reachable in steps of 3.

Animal Jumps Q2, p.128 ("Squirrel jumps 4 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? How many jumps to reach 60?") — Students complete the 4-step line, then answer the jump-count question, comparing strategies with a partner.

Animal Jumps Q3, p.129 ("Rabbit jumps 6 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? What is the smallest 3-digit number it lands on? How many jumps?") — Students extend the 6-step pattern beyond the printed ovals to locate the first 3-digit multiple. Brief whole-class share.

periods.teacher_notes: The key idea is that skip counting produces multiples — every number the animal lands on is a multiple of its step size. A common error is treating every number on the line as a landing spot; redirect by asking 'did the animal step here, or did it jump over?' The 67-is-not-a-multiple-of-3 inquiry is the conceptual anchor of this unit.
materials: counters or coins for marking hops

section_titles: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
periods.activity_title: Two Animals, One Landing — Finding Common Multiples

tasks_in_class.description: Kangaroo jumps 8 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? Are there numbers both the rabbit and kangaroo will touch?
To reach 48, how many times did the rabbit jump? How many times did the kangaroo jump? What did you observe?
Which numbers do both the frog and the squirrel touch? A few common multiples of 3 and 4 are ___.
Cat on 6, rat on 12. Cat jumps 3 steps, rat jumps 2 steps. Will the cat catch the rat? If yes, at which number?

time_bands.activity: Animal Jumps Q4, p.129 ("Kangaroo jumps 8 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? Are there numbers both the rabbit and kangaroo will touch?") — Students fill the 8-step line, then circle numbers shared with the 6-step rabbit line from skip counting built on earlier.

Animal Jumps Q5, p.129 ("To reach 48, how many times did the rabbit jump? How many times did the kangaroo jump? What did you observe?") — Students count jumps to 48 on each line and compare; class discussion on why 48 is reachable by both animals.

Common Multiples Q1, p.130 ("Which numbers do both the frog and the squirrel touch? A few common multiples of 3 and 4 are ___.") — Students list shared landings from their two number lines and name them common multiples. Pairs share their lists.

Common Multiples Q7, p.130 ("Cat on 6, rat on 12. Cat jumps 3 steps, rat jumps 2 steps. Will the cat catch the rat? If yes, at which number?") — Students act out the chase on a number strip, reasoning about when both paths meet; whole-class discussion of the result.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on students' filled number lines for steps of 6 and 8, the overlapping landings are the concrete entry into common multiples. A frequent confusion is listing all multiples of one animal as 'common'; insist students check the second animal's line. The cat-and-rat chase deepens this by requiring simultaneous tracking of two step sequences.

section_titles: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
periods.activity_title: From Shared Landings to Equal Rows — Arrays in the Garden

tasks_in_class.description: Which numbers do both the rabbit and the kangaroo touch? A few common multiples of 6 and 8 are ___.
12 lily flowers, each with 3 petals. How many petals? Use the 10+2 break-apart strategy.
Gulabo plants marigold saplings in a box. Count rows and columns from the picture. Write the mathematical statement.
Dailyfresh supermarket keeps strawberry boxes in a tray. Count columns and boxes per column from picture. Write the mathematical statement.

time_bands.activity: Common Multiples Q2, p.130 ("Which numbers do both the rabbit and the kangaroo touch? A few common multiples of 6 and 8 are ___.") — Students use their 6-step and 8-step lines to list common landings, consolidating the idea of common multiples before the section closes.

Gulabo's Garden Q1, p.131 ("12 lily flowers, each with 3 petals. How many petals? Use the 10+2 break-apart strategy.") — Teacher models breaking 12 into 10+2, computing 10×3 and 2×3 separately, then summing. Students try with a different pair of numbers.

Gulabo's Garden Q3, p.132 ("Gulabo plants marigold saplings in a box. Count rows and columns from the picture. Write the mathematical statement.") — Students examine the picture, count rows and columns, and record a multiplication sentence. Pairs compare and discuss if they wrote rows×columns or columns×rows.

Gulabo's Garden Q4, p.132 ("Dailyfresh supermarket keeps strawberry boxes in a tray. Count columns and boxes per column from picture. Write the mathematical statement.") — Students repeat the counting-and-recording process with the strawberry array and share sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: The shift from number lines to arrays is the central move of this unit — multiplication is now seen as rows times columns, not only repeated counting. Students often write only one orientation (e.g. 4×6 but not 6×4); prompt them to write both and notice the product is the same. The 10+2 strategy for 12×3 previews the break-apart work that deepens in later sections.
materials: grid paper or dot arrays for hands-on counting

section_titles: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
periods.activity_title: Cupcake Trays — Multiple Arrangements of the Same Number

tasks_in_class.description: Complete arranging 18 cupcakes in two differently shaped trays given below.
She can use two such trays in her oven at a time. How many cupcakes can she make in one attempt?
She has received a special order and made 108 cupcakes. How many trays has she baked?
Square baking tray holds 36 mini cupcakes. Complete the arrangement. Write number of columns, cupcakes per column, and multiplication statement.
Find different ways of arranging 36, 8, 12, and 24 cupcakes in rows and columns in your notebook.

homework.description: Hibiscus has 5 petals. Gulabo counted 80 petals. How many flowers? Use the 5→10→50 build-up strategy.

time_bands.activity: Gulabo's Garden Q5a, p.132 ("Complete arranging 18 cupcakes in two differently shaped trays given below.") — Students draw dot-arrays for the two tray shapes and write both multiplication sentences (e.g. 6×3 and 9×2), seeing that the same quantity has multiple array forms.

Gulabo's Garden Q5b, p.133 ("She can use two such trays in her oven at a time. How many cupcakes can she make in one attempt?") and Q5c, p.133 ("She has received a special order and made 108 cupcakes. How many trays has she baked?") — Students solve both, recognising Q5c as division as the inverse of multiplication.

Gulabo's Garden Q5d, p.133 ("Square baking tray holds 36 mini cupcakes. Complete the arrangement. Write number of columns, cupcakes per column, and multiplication statement.") — Students complete the square array, noting that equal rows and equal columns produce a square arrangement.

Gulabo's Garden (open task), p.133 ("Find different ways of arranging 36, 8, 12, and 24 cupcakes in rows and columns in your notebook.") — Students list as many row×column pairs as they can find in the time available and compare lists with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes write only one arrangement per number; encourage them to ask 'can I make a different rectangle?' to find all factor pairs. The division in Q5c (108÷18) connects multiplication and division as inverse operations — stress that finding the number of trays is the reverse of filling them. Q5d's square array is a special case worth naming explicitly.

periods.activity_title: Magician Anvi's Double — Even Ones Digits Always

tasks_in_class.description: Anvi doubled 23 flowers. How many are there now? Complete the before-and-after magic table for 10, 51, 95, 150, 199, 425, 500 and reverse for 222, 410, 500.
Guess the ones digit of the following numbers when doubled: 28, 56, 45, 17.
Give examples of numbers that when doubled give 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 in the ones place. Can we get 3, 5, 7, 9? Even or odd?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the magic trick: teacher holds up 23 counters, 'doubles' them by adding 23 more, and asks students to predict the result. Connect to multiplication as 2×23. Students start the before-and-after table from The Doubling Magic (opening), p.134 ("Anvi doubled 23 flowers. How many are there now? Complete the before-and-after magic table…") for the given values.

Continue The Doubling Magic (opening), p.134 — students complete the reverse section (halving 222, 410, 500), then briefly discuss how they found the 'before' value. Dienes blocks may be used for 3-digit doublings.

The Doubling Magic Q1, p.134 ("Guess the ones digit of the following numbers when doubled: 28, 56, 45, 17.") — Students guess first, then verify by computing. Class collects all ones digits on the board.

The Doubling Magic Q2, p.134 ("Give examples of numbers that when doubled give 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 in the ones place. Can we get 3, 5, 7, 9? Even or odd?") — Students generate examples and try to force an odd ones digit, leading to the generalisation that doubled numbers are always even.

periods.teacher_notes: The central generalisation is that any whole number doubled produces an even result, so the ones digit can only be 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Students often guess 5 is possible when starting from 5 (5+5=10, ones digit 0); use this as evidence, not a counter-example. Dienes blocks or a ganit mala help students see the doubling physically before moving to symbolic computation.

periods.activity_title: The 10×10 Chart — Filling In and Noticing Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Fill each square in the 10×10 chart by multiplying the row number by the column number.
What do you notice about the numbers shaded in green? Why is this happening?
Share the patterns that you notice in the table.
Are the numbers in row 7 the same as in column 7? In general, are numbers in a given row the same as in the corresponding column? Why?

time_bands.activity: Multiplication Table (chart fill), p.135 ("Fill each square in the 10×10 chart by multiplying the row number by the column number.") — Students work silently to complete the chart; teacher circulates watching for computation errors.

Multiplication Table (green shading), p.135 ("What do you notice about the numbers shaded in green? Why is this happening?") — Students examine the shaded diagonal and articulate what is special about those products; pairs share ideas.

Multiplication Table Q1, p.135 ("Share the patterns that you notice in the table.") — Open invitation for students to name any pattern they see: rows, columns, diagonal, evens/odds. List contributions on the board without evaluating yet.

Multiplication Table Q2, p.135 ("Are the numbers in row 7 the same as in column 7? In general, are numbers in a given row the same as in the corresponding column? Why?") — Students verify with two or three rows and columns, then articulate commutativity in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The completed 10×10 chart is the reference tool for the pattern investigations; accuracy in filling it matters. The green shading highlights the symmetry axis (commutative pairs), which gives students a visual entry into Q2. A common error is claiming row 7 and column 7 are 'the same thing' without explaining why; press for the multiplicative reason.
materials: 10×10 multiplication chart (textbook p.135 or printed worksheet)

periods.activity_title: Even, Odd, and Ones-Digit Cycles in the Chart

tasks_in_class.description: Is there a row where all products are even numbers? Which rows have this property?
Is there a row having only odd numbers as products?
Are there rows that have both even and odd numbers? What do you notice? Why is it so?
Observe the pattern in the ones digits of products in row 5. Observe other rows. What patterns do you notice?
Row 8 ones digits: 8,6,4,2,0,8,6,4,2,0. Guess the ones digit of 11×8, 12×8, 13×8. Verify by multiplying.

homework.description: Colour the common multiples of (a) 2 and 3, (b) 4 and 8, (c) 7 and 9 using different colours. Share observations.

time_bands.activity: Multiplication Table Q3, p.135 ("Is there a row where all products are even numbers? Which rows have this property?") and Q4, p.135 ("Is there a row having only odd numbers as products?") — Students circle all-even rows and look for an all-odd row; groups share findings and give reasons.

Multiplication Table Q5, p.135 ("Are there rows that have both even and odd numbers? What do you notice? Why is it so?") — Students identify mixed rows and reason about the structure: an odd multiplier times an even number gives even, times an odd gives odd.

Multiplication Table Q8, p.136 ("Observe the pattern in the ones digits of products in row 5. Observe other rows. What patterns do you notice?") — Students extract and write just the ones digits for rows 5, 2, and 8, looking for repeating cycles.

Multiplication Table Q9, p.136 ("Row 8 ones digits: 8,6,4,2,0,8,6,4,2,0. Guess the ones digit of 11×8, 12×8, 13×8. Verify by multiplying.") — Students use the cycle to predict beyond the table, then verify, experiencing how a pattern extends.

periods.teacher_notes: The key generalisation in Q3–Q5 is that a row produces all-even products only when its multiplier is even; row 7 produces all-odd products because 7 is odd and odd×odd=odd. Students often claim row 1 is all-odd, which is true — ask them to explain why using the even/odd rule. The ones-digit cycle in row 8 is the chapter's main extension-prediction task.
materials: Completed 10×10 chart from previous work or textbook p.135

periods.activity_title: Closing the Chart, Opening the Tens — Multiplying by 10s

tasks_in_class.description: Is there a row in which all the digits from 0 to 9 appear as the ones digit? Which rows have this property?
Count wheels in 10 tricycles (10×3), 10 more tricycles, and 20 tricycles. Fill blanks and notice the pattern.
Count wheels in 10 cars (10×4) and 30 cars (30×4). Fill blanks and notice the pattern.

time_bands.activity: Multiplication Table Q11, p.136 ("Is there a row in which all the digits from 0 to 9 appear as the ones digit? Which rows have this property?") — Students scan ones-digit lists they assembled earlier and identify the rows where every digit 0–9 appears; brief class discussion on why this happens for certain rows.

Multiples of Tens Q1, p.137 ("Count wheels in 10 tricycles (10×3), 10 more tricycles, and 20 tricycles. Fill blanks and notice the pattern.") — Students build the count by grouping: 10×3=30, another 10×3=30, so 20×3=60. Teacher articulates 'ten-times' language.

Multiples of Tens Q2, p.137 ("Count wheels in 10 cars (10×4) and 30 cars (30×4). Fill blanks and notice the pattern.") — Students extend to a multiple-of-ten that is larger (30×4), reasoning about three groups of 10.

Multiples of Tens (solve set), p.137 ("Solve in a similar way: 10×6, 40×6, 10×8, 60×8, 6×8, 60×8, 4×6, 40×8.") — Students practise the pattern with varied pairs, recording each step and checking against the basic fact.

periods.teacher_notes: The Q11 closure completes the ones-digit investigation thread; rows 3, 7, 9, and 1 produce all 10 distinct ones digits because they are coprime to 10. For the Multiples of Tens section, the key language is 'twenty threes is the same as ten threes twice' — encourage students to say this before writing numerals. Watch for students writing 20×3=6 (dropping the zero); connect to place value.
materials: small wheeled toys or pictures of tricycles/cars (optional)

periods.activity_title: Break It at Ten — Multiplying 2-Digit Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Radha packs cupcakes in boxes of 4. She has packed 18 boxes. How many cupcakes? Use 10+8 decomposition.
8 bamboo rods needed for each bullock cart. How many rods for 23 carts? Use 20+3 decomposition.
25 geese and 12 sheep around a pond. Chippi the lizard sees many legs. How many legs does it see?
8 children sitting in each row, 15 such rows in an auditorium. How many children are in the auditorium?

homework.description: A book shop has 9 books in each pile and 14 such piles. How many books does the shop have?

time_bands.activity: Multiplying Using 10s Q1, p.138 ("Radha packs cupcakes in boxes of 4. She has packed 18 boxes. How many cupcakes? Use 10+8 decomposition.") — Teacher works through the structured table: 10×4=40, 8×4=32, total 72. Students copy and discuss why decomposing at ten is efficient.

Multiplying Using 10s Q2, p.139 ("8 bamboo rods needed for each bullock cart. How many rods for 23 carts? Use 20+3 decomposition.") — Students set up their own table for 23×8, using 20+3. Pairs compare tables before a class check.

Let Us Solve Q1, p.139 ("25 geese and 12 sheep around a pond. Chippi the lizard sees many legs. How many legs does it see?") — Students identify 25×2 (bird legs) + 12×4 (sheep legs), decomposing each multiplicand at ten.

Let Us Solve Q2, p.139 ("8 children sitting in each row, 15 such rows in an auditorium. How many children are in the auditorium?") — Students apply 15×8 = 10×8 + 5×8 and record the answer. Quick class comparison of results.

periods.teacher_notes: The partial-product table is the scaffold for all 2-digit × 1-digit work in this chapter; insist students show both partial products before adding. A common error is computing only 10×(single digit) and forgetting the ones part (e.g. writing 18×4=40 instead of 40+32=72). Q1 from Let Us Solve is a two-step problem — students must identify two separate multiplication sentences before summing.

periods.activity_title: Taking Away Groups — The Partial Quotient Method

tasks_in_class.description: Factory ordered 58 wheels for tempos, each with 3 wheels. How many tempos can be made? Discuss thinking at each step.
Dairy farm: Chippi sees 88 legs. How many cows? Show work using the table, taking out groups of 10s.
In a big aquarium, Jolly fish sees 72 legs of octopuses. How many octopuses are there?
Sports store packs 4 shuttlecocks in a box. They have 50 shuttlecocks. How many full boxes? How many are left?

homework.description: Rakul Chachi planted 75 rose saplings with 5 saplings per row. How many rows has she planted?

time_bands.activity: Division Q1, p.140 ("Factory ordered 58 wheels for tempos, each with 3 wheels. How many tempos can be made? Discuss thinking at each step.") — Teacher models the step-by-step table: take 10×3=30 away from 58 (28 left), take another 9×3=27 away (1 left), total 19 tempos with 1 wheel remaining.

Division Q2, p.141 ("Dairy farm: Chippi sees 88 legs. How many cows? Show work using the table, taking out groups of 10s.") — Students set up their own table for 88÷4, deciding how many groups of 10 to remove at each step.

Let Us Solve Q1, p.141 ("In a big aquarium, Jolly fish sees 72 legs of octopuses. How many octopuses are there?") — Students recognise octopuses have 8 legs, set up 72÷8, and apply partial quotient. Groups share strategies.

Let Us Solve Q2, p.141 ("Sports store packs 4 shuttlecocks in a box. They have 50 shuttlecocks. How many full boxes? How many are left?") — Students practise with a non-zero remainder, naming the quotient and the remainder separately.

periods.teacher_notes: Distinguish the two kinds of division problems the textbook names: share problems (how many in each group?) and measure problems (how many groups?). Students sometimes stop at the first step of partial quotient and give an incomplete answer — press them to continue subtracting until no full group remains. Remainders are part of the answer and should always be stated.

periods.activity_title: Hundreds in a Grid — Multiplying by 100s and 3-Digit Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: 100 bikes with 2 people each, 200 bikes; 100 cars with 4 people each, 500 cars. Fill in the blanks and describe how you found it.
125 autorickshaws carry 8 passengers each. How many passengers total? Use 100+20+5 decomposition.
Kahlu and Rabia pack 6 kulhads per box and packed 174 boxes. How many kulhads total? Use 100+70+4 decomposition.

time_bands.activity: Multiples of 100 (bikes and cars), p.142 ("100 bikes with 2 people each, 200 bikes; 100 cars with 4 people each, 500 cars. Fill in the blanks and describe how you found it.") — Students explore the 10×10 dot grid for 100 bikes, see that 100×2 follows the same scaling as 10×2, and describe the 'hundred-times' pattern.

Multiples of 100 (pattern table), p.143 ("Observe the pattern and complete: 1×3, 10×3, 100×3; …") — Students complete the full fact-family table, articulating the pattern in words before writing numerals.

More Multiplication Q1, p.143-144 ("125 autorickshaws carry 8 passengers each. How many passengers total? Use 100+20+5 decomposition.") — Teacher models 100×8 + 20×8 + 5×8 using the structured partial-product table; students record each partial product.

More Multiplication Q2, p.144 ("Kahlu and Rabia pack 6 kulhads per box and packed 174 boxes. How many kulhads total? Use 100+70+4 decomposition.") — Students set up and solve 174×6 independently, applying the three-part decomposition.

periods.teacher_notes: The pattern-table exercise connects the 'ten-times' structure from Multiples of Tens to 'hundred-times', building place-value reasoning as a multiplication tool. When extending to 3-digit multiplicands, students sometimes add partial products in the wrong column — insist they name the partial product fully (e.g. '100 times 8 is 800') before writing. Q2's kulhad context introduces a ones digit (4) that requires a separate partial product.

periods.activity_title: Real-World Multiplying and Dividing with Larger Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: BP Girl's school has 465 students and gives each two pencils on the first day. How many pencils does the school need to buy?
9 boats ferry 108 people equally. How many people per boat? Use partial quotient method (5+5+2).
7 buses take 245 children to the transport museum, each bus carrying the same number. How many children in each bus?
Anu saves ₹45 every month. (a) How much in 6 months? (b) Distribute total among 6 friends, how much each? (c) Distribute among 3 friends, how much each?
Raju makes 8 auto trips a day. Which questions can be exactly calculated: (a) money per day? (b) trips in 7 days? (c) time per trip? (d) trips in 4 weeks?

homework.description: 234 children organise a school mela, each contributing ₹5. How much money do they collect?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q1, p.144 ("BP Girl's school has 465 students and gives each two pencils on the first day. How many pencils does the school need to buy?") — Students apply 3-digit decomposition (400+60+5)×2 and record partial products.

More Division (Cauvery ferry), p.145 ("9 boats ferry 108 people equally. How many people per boat? Use partial quotient method (5+5+2).") — Teacher models 108÷9 using the step table: 5×9=45 away (63 left), 5×9=45 away (18 left), 2×9=18 away (0 left), total 12 per boat.

Let Us Solve Q1, p.147 ("7 buses take 245 children to the transport museum, each bus carrying the same number. How many children in each bus?") — Students set up 245÷7 using partial quotient, deciding on convenient group sizes.

Let Us Solve Q4, p.147 ("Anu saves ₹45 every month. (a) How much in 6 months? (b) Distribute total among 6 friends, how much each? (c) Distribute among 3 friends, how much each?") — Students solve all three parts, seeing how multiplication and division interact in a single connected problem.

Let Us Solve Q5, p.147 ("Raju makes 8 auto trips a day. Which questions can be exactly calculated: …?") — Quick whole-class discussion: students distinguish which questions have a determinate answer from given information and which require additional data.

periods.teacher_notes: The Cauvery ferry problem demonstrates that the partial quotient approach works for 3-digit dividends: choosing 5 groups at each step keeps the arithmetic manageable. In Q4, students often solve (a) correctly but confuse (b) and (c) — remind them that the dividend for (b) is the answer to (a). Q5 develops critical reading of a problem, an important mathematical habit.
materials: pencils and paper for multi-step working

periods.activity_title: Always, Never, Sometimes — Patterns in Dividing by 10s and 100s

tasks_in_class.description: Tick always/never/sometimes true: multiplying by 10 gives 0 in ones; ×2 gives odd; ×5 gives 5 in ones; number after odd is even; halving any number gives even; adding 0 increases by 1.
₹30 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? ₹900 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? Draw arrows linking money and children.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Patterns in Division (sets A, B, C), p.146

tasks_in_class.description: Solve: (1) 60 tyres ÷ 6 = how many trucks? (2) 80 wheels ÷ 4 = how many cars? (3) 600 ant legs ÷ 6 = how many ants? (4) 800 rubber bands ÷ 4 rubber bands per packet = how many packets?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q7, p.148 ("Tick always/never/sometimes true: multiplying by 10 gives 0 in ones; ×2 gives odd; ×5 gives 5 in ones; number after odd is even; halving any number gives even; adding 0 increases by 1.") — Students work individually then discuss; for each 'sometimes' answer, they supply one true and one false example.

Patterns in Division Q1-2, p.146 ("₹30 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? ₹900 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? Draw arrows linking money and children.") — Students solve both, draw arrows, and articulate how 300÷3 follows directly from 3÷3 by place-value scaling.

Patterns in Division (sets A, B, C), p.146 ("Observe and explain patterns. Complete: A: 3÷3, 30÷3, 300÷3; …") — Students complete all three sets, then write in their own words the pattern they see when dividing multiples of 10 or 100.

Patterns in Division (word problems), p.146 ("Solve: (1) 60 tyres ÷ 6 = how many trucks? …") — Students apply the pattern to each word problem, naming the basic fact they used (e.g. 6÷6=1 → 60÷6=10) before writing the answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The always/never/sometimes table is a critical-thinking task that draws together patterns — ones-digit behaviour, doubling, and even/odd results. Students frequently mark '×5 gives 5 in ones' as always true; probe with 10×5=50 (ones digit 0). For the division patterns, anchor each answer to its basic fact to make the scaling explicit rather than procedural.

25 geese and 12 sheep around a pond. Chippi the lizard sees many legs. How many legs does it see?
Factory ordered 58 wheels for tempos, each with 3 wheels. How many tempos can be made? Discuss thinking at each step.
Sports store packs 4 shuttlecocks in a box. They have 50 shuttlecocks. How many full boxes? How many are left?

Solve: (1) 60 tyres ÷ 6 = how many trucks? (2) 80 wheels ÷ 4 = how many cars? (3) 600 ant legs ÷ 6 = how many ants? (4) 800 rubber bands ÷ 4 rubber bands per packet = how many packets?

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: Draw 3 rows of 5 dots in your notebook to show marigold saplings planted in equal rows. Write the multiplication statement for your drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A 3×5 array of dots; multiplication statement: 3 × 5 = 15 (or 5 × 3 = 15).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count rows and columns in the drawn array and write rows × columns = total.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use counters or seeds to make the array first; stretch: ask them to draw a second arrangement that also has 15.

exercise.description: Gulabo plants marigold saplings in a box. Count rows and columns from the picture. Write the mathematical statement.

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: Radha arranges 18 cupcakes in a tray with 6 cupcakes in each row. How many rows does she make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 rows (because 3 × 6 = 18).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find how many equal groups of 6 fit into 18 by counting up: 6, 12, 18 — three groups.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have halved 6 instead of dividing 18 by 6.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have added 18 + 6 or guessed without checking.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confused the group size (6) with the number of groups.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw 18 dots and circle groups of 6; stretch: ask how the answer changes if there are 7 cupcakes per row.

exercise.description: Complete arranging 18 cupcakes in two differently shaped trays given below.

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: In your notebook, show two different ways to arrange 24 cupcakes in equal rows and columns. Write the multiplication statement for each way.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two correct factor pairs of 24, for example: 4 × 6 = 24 and 3 × 8 = 24 (other valid pairs: 2×12, 1×24, 6×4, 8×3, etc.).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a number that divides 24 evenly to form one dimension, then compute the other dimension.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student counters to physically rearrange; stretch: ask them to find all possible arrangements.

exercise.description: Find different ways of arranging 36, 8, 12, and 24 cupcakes in rows and columns in your notebook.

items.prompt: A bus has 4 wheels. Fill in the blanks: 10 buses have ___ wheels. 20 buses have ___ wheels. Explain how you moved from the first answer to the second.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 10 buses: 40 wheels; 20 buses: 80 wheels. Explanation: 20 buses is twice 10 buses, so 40 + 40 = 80.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute 10 × 4 = 40, then double it for 20 × 4 = 80.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw 10 groups of 4 dots first; stretch: ask how many wheels 30 buses would have.

exercise.description: Count wheels in 10 tricycles (10×3), 10 more tricycles, and 20 tricycles. Fill blanks and notice the pattern.

items.prompt: A rickshaw carries 3 people. How many people do 100 rickshaws carry? How many do 300 rickshaws carry? Write both answers and explain the pattern you see.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 100 rickshaws: 300 people; 300 rickshaws: 900 people. Pattern: each hundred rickshaws adds 300 people, so 300 rickshaws carry three times as many as 100 rickshaws.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use 100 × 3 = 300 and scale by three hundreds to get 300 × 3 = 900.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student first solve 1×3, 10×3, then 100×3 in steps; stretch: ask how many people 500 rickshaws carry.

exercise.description: 100 bikes with 2 people each, 200 bikes; 100 cars with 4 people each, 500 cars. Fill in the blanks and describe how you found it.

items.section_title: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
items.prompt: A frog jumps 3 steps at a time starting from 0. Will it ever land on the number 52? Choose the correct answer and the best reason.

options.label: A
options.text: No, because 52 is not a multiple of 3.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because 52 is too large for the frog.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, because 52 comes after 51 which is a multiple of 3.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, because 52 is an even number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No, because 52 is not a multiple of 3 (51 = 17×3, 54 = 18×3; 52 is between them).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether 52 is reachable by listing multiples of 3 near 52: 51 and 54, so 52 is skipped.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses even/odd with divisibility by 3.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student thinks landing near a multiple means landing on it; does not understand the exact skip-count rule.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has no mathematical reason and relies on an informal guess.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student continue the 3-skip sequence on a number line to 54 and check; stretch: ask whether 99 is a multiple of 3 and how they know.

exercise.description: Frog jumps 3 steps at a time. Which numbers will the frog touch? Will it touch 67?

items.section_title: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
items.prompt: A rabbit jumps 6 steps and a kangaroo jumps 8 steps, both starting at 0. They both land on 48. How many jumps did the rabbit take? How many did the kangaroo take? Which animal reached 48 in fewer jumps? Explain why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rabbit: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 jumps. Kangaroo: 48 ÷ 8 = 6 jumps. The kangaroo reached 48 in fewer jumps because each kangaroo jump is larger (8 steps vs 6 steps), so fewer jumps are needed to cover the same distance.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 48 by each jump size to count the number of jumps, then compare.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student mark both skip sequences on a number line and count; stretch: ask at what other number do both animals land, and how many jumps each takes to get there.

exercise.description: To reach 48, how many times did the rabbit jump? How many times did the kangaroo jump? What did you observe?

items.section_title: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
items.prompt: A deer jumps 8 steps at a time. A goat jumps 6 steps at a time. Both start at 0. Name two numbers where both animals will land. How did you find them?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two correct common multiples of 6 and 8 (e.g. 24 and 48). Students should list multiples of 6 and multiples of 8 and identify shared values.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 8 (8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, …) and check which appear in multiples of 6 (6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, …).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide printed number lines for 6-steps and 8-steps and ask the student to circle shared numbers; stretch: ask whether both animals will ever land on 40 and explain why or why not.

exercise.description: Kangaroo jumps 8 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? Are there numbers both the rabbit and kangaroo will touch?

items.prompt: A cat is at number 9 and a mouse is at number 15. The cat jumps 3 steps at a time and the mouse jumps 2 steps at a time. Will the cat ever catch the mouse? If yes, at which number? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cat's positions after jumps: 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, … Mouse's positions: 15, 17, 19, 21, … Both reach 21 (cat after 4 more jumps from 9; mouse after 3 more jumps from 15). Yes, the cat catches the mouse at 21.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List successive positions of both animals and find the first number that appears on both lists.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a number line and two different coloured pencils to mark each animal's jumps; stretch: change the cat's starting position to 6 and ask whether the answer changes.

exercise.description: Cat on 6, rat on 12. Cat jumps 3 steps, rat jumps 2 steps. Will the cat catch the rat? If yes, at which number?

items.prompt: Anvi doubles the number 37. What will be the ones digit of the result?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4. Double of 37 is 74, ones digit is 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Double only the ones digit: 7 + 7 = 14, ones digit is 4.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have written the tens digit of 37 or confused with the original number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student repeated the ones digit of 37 without doubling it.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have confused doubling with adding 5, or linked to ×5 rule.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use a number line or beads to physically double the ones digit; stretch: ask which ones digits are impossible after doubling and explain why.

exercise.description: Guess the ones digit of the following numbers when doubled: 28, 56, 45, 17.

items.prompt: Priya says: 'When I double any number, the answer always has an even ones digit.' Is Priya correct? Give two examples to support your answer, and explain why this is always true.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Priya is correct. Examples: double of 13 = 26 (ones digit 6), double of 9 = 18 (ones digit 8). Doubling means ×2; any number times 2 is even, so the ones digit must be 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiplying by 2 always produces an even number, so the ones digit can only be 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student list doubles of 1–10 and circle the ones digits; stretch: ask whether tripling a number always gives an odd ones digit and explain.

exercise.description: Give examples of numbers that when doubled give 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 in the ones place. Can we get 3, 5, 7, 9? Even or odd?

items.prompt: Look at the multiplication table. Is the product 5 × 9 the same as the product 9 × 5? Write both products. Explain in one sentence why this is true for any two numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 × 9 = 45 and 9 × 5 = 45. This is true for any two numbers because multiplying in any order gives the same total (the order of the groups does not change how many there are altogether).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Row 5 column 9 and row 9 column 5 of the multiplication table are equal — the table is symmetric about its diagonal.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw a 5×9 array and rotate it to see it is the same as 9×5; stretch: ask whether this rule works for three numbers (e.g. 2×3×4 vs 4×3×2).

exercise.description: Are the numbers in row 7 the same as in column 7? In general, are numbers in a given row the same as in the corresponding column? Why?

items.prompt: In the multiplication table, which of the following rows contains ONLY even numbers?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 4. Multiplying any whole number by 4 (an even number) always gives an even product.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: An even number times any whole number is always even; row 4 is an even multiplier so all its products are even.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may not have checked: 3×1=3, 3×3=9 are odd; row 3 has both even and odd products.
what_each_option_reveals.C: 7 is odd, so 7×1=7 and 7×3=21 are odd; row 7 has only odd products.
what_each_option_reveals.D: 9 is odd, so row 9 has both even and odd products.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student list the first five products in row 4 and circle each as even or odd; stretch: ask how many rows in the 10×10 table contain only even numbers and name them all.

exercise.description: Is there a row where all products are even numbers? Which rows have this property?

items.prompt: The ones digits in row 8 of the multiplication table follow the pattern 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, 8, 6, 4, 2, 0. What will be the ones digit of 14 × 8? Explain how you used the pattern.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The ones digit of 14 × 8 is 2. The cycle length is 5 (positions 1–5 then repeats). Position 14: 14 = 10 + 4, and position 4 in the cycle has digit 2. Verify: 14 × 8 = 112, ones digit 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify where position 14 falls in the repeating cycle 8-6-4-2-0 to read off the ones digit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write out the cycle and count to position 14 by continuing the pattern; stretch: ask for the ones digit of 23 × 8.

exercise.description: Row 8 ones digits: 8,6,4,2,0,8,6,4,2,0. Guess the ones digit of 11×8, 12×8, 13×8. Verify by multiplying.

items.prompt: In the multiplication table, which row shows all ten digits (0 through 9) appearing as the ones digit of its products?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 3. The ones digits of 1×3 through 10×3 are 3, 6, 9, 2, 5, 8, 1, 4, 7, 0 — all ten digits appear.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List the ones digits of each product in row 3 and check that every digit 0–9 appears exactly once in the first 10 products.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Row 2 only produces even ones digits (2,4,6,8,0) — only 5 distinct digits.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Row 5 only produces 5 and 0 as ones digits — only 2 distinct digits.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Row 4 produces 4,8,2,6,0 — only 5 distinct even digits.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a written list of products for row 3 and ask them to circle the ones digit of each; stretch: ask the student to find another row with the same property and explain why it works.

exercise.description: Is there a row in which all the digits from 0 to 9 appear as the ones digit? Which rows have this property?

items.prompt: ₹60 is shared equally among 3 children. How much does each child get? Now ₹600 is shared equally among 3 children. How much does each child get? Explain the pattern you see.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 60 ÷ 3 = 20; 600 ÷ 3 = 200. Pattern: when the dividend is multiplied by 10, the quotient is also multiplied by 10 — the basic fact 6 ÷ 3 = 2 scales with the place value of the dividend.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the basic fact 6 ÷ 3 = 2, then apply place-value scaling: 60 ÷ 3 = 20 and 600 ÷ 3 = 200.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw arrows linking each money amount to its quotient as shown in the textbook; stretch: ask what 6000 ÷ 3 would be using the same pattern.

exercise.description: ₹30 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? ₹900 shared equally among 3 children — how much each? Draw arrows linking money and children.

items.prompt: Riya says: 'When you multiply a number by 5, the ones digit is always 5.' Is this always true, never true, or sometimes true?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sometimes true. When multiplying an odd number by 5 the ones digit is 5 (e.g. 3×5=15), but when multiplying an even number by 5 the ones digit is 0 (e.g. 4×5=20).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check row 5 of the multiplication table: products alternate between ones digits of 5 and 0.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not considered even multipliers (e.g. 2×5=10, ones digit 0).
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have only recalled cases where the ones digit is 0 and overgeneralised.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Partially correct reasoning — the ones digit is 5 for odd multipliers — but the phrasing excludes the correct conclusion that it is sometimes (not always) true.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student list 1×5 through 10×5 and circle the ones digits; stretch: ask what ones digits are possible when multiplying by 5 and prove each case.

exercise.description: Tick always/never/sometimes true: multiplying by 10 gives 0 in ones; ×2 gives odd; ×5 gives 5 in ones; number after odd is even; halving any number gives even; adding 0 increases by 1.

items.section_title: Animal Jumps — skip counting and multiples
items.prompt: A squirrel jumps 4 steps at a time starting from 0. How many jumps does it need to reach 36?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 36 by the step size 4 to count the number of jumps.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have subtracted 4 from 36 and divided the remainder, or confused with a different divisor.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have computed 32 ÷ 4 = 8 and stopped one step early.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have added one extra jump or computed 40 ÷ 4.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student fill in a skip-count sequence 0, 4, 8, … and count the steps to 36; stretch: ask how many jumps are needed to reach 60.

exercise.description: Squirrel jumps 4 steps at a time. Which numbers will it touch? How many jumps to reach 60?

items.prompt: Magician Anvi had 145 beads. She doubled them. How many beads does she have now?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use Dienes blocks or written partial products (double hundreds, double tens, double ones separately) then add; stretch: ask what the result would be if she doubled 290 again.

exercise.description: Anvi doubled 23 flowers. How many are there now? Complete the before-and-after magic table for 10, 51, 95, 150, 199, 425, 500 and reverse for 222, 410, 500.

items.prompt: What is the product of 7 × 8?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate row 7, column 8 in the multiplication table.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have computed 6 × 8 instead of 7 × 8.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have computed 6 × 9 or confused with 54.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have computed 7 × 9 instead of 7 × 8.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use the filled 10×10 chart to look up the product; stretch: ask what 17 × 8 equals using the ones-digit pattern from row 8.

exercise.description: Fill each square in the 10×10 chart by multiplying the row number by the column number.

items.prompt: What is 50 × 6?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the basic fact 5 × 6 = 30 and scale by ten to get 50 × 6 = 300.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student simply added 50 and 6 instead of multiplying.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student computed the basic fact 5 × 6 = 30 but forgot the ten-times scaling.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student first compute 5 × 6 and then say 'fifty is ten fives, so multiply by ten'; stretch: ask what 70 × 6 equals using the same method.

items.prompt: Complete: 300 × 4 = ___. Show the two partial steps you used.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the basic fact 3 × 4 = 12, then scale by one hundred: 300 × 4 = 1200.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student first write the pattern triple 3×4, 30×4, 300×4 and observe each step; stretch: ask what 300 × 7 equals without writing intermediate steps.

items.prompt: What is 900 ÷ 9?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use 9 ÷ 9 = 1 and scale by one hundred: 900 ÷ 9 = 100.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have computed 90 ÷ 9 = 10 (one place value step instead of two).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student gave the divisor as the answer, confusing it with the quotient.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student complete the sequence 9÷9, 90÷9, 900÷9 step by step; stretch: ask what 9000 ÷ 9 would be.

exercise.book_ref: Patterns in Division (sets A, B, C), p.146

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: A sunflower has 8 petals. Gulabo counts 96 petals in total. How many sunflowers are there? Use a build-up strategy to find your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12 sunflowers. 10 × 8 = 80; 2 × 8 = 16; 80 + 16 = 96; so 12 sunflowers.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build up from 10 groups of 8 (=80), then find how many more groups of 8 make 96.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw a table with 'groups' and 'petals' columns, filling in 10 groups first; stretch: ask what happens if each flower had 9 petals and there were 108 petals total.

exercise.description: 12 lily flowers, each with 3 petals. How many petals? Use the 10+2 break-apart strategy.

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: A baker puts 9 muffins in each tray. She uses 4 trays. How many muffins can she bake in one go?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 36 muffins. 4 × 9 = 36.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply number of trays by muffins per tray: 4 × 9 = 36.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw 4 rows of 9 dots and count; stretch: ask how many trays she needs to bake 63 muffins.

exercise.description: She can use two such trays in her oven at a time. How many cupcakes can she make in one attempt?

items.section_title: Gulabo's Garden — multiplication as equal groups
items.prompt: A baker baked 126 cupcakes using trays that hold 18 cupcakes each. How many trays did she use?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total cupcakes by the tray capacity: 126 ÷ 18 = 7.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student count up in 18s (18, 36, 54, 72, 90, 108, 126) and count the steps; stretch: ask how many trays are needed for 162 cupcakes.

exercise.description: She has received a special order and made 108 cupcakes. How many trays has she baked?

items.prompt: A teacher packs 6 crayons in each box. She packs 19 boxes. How many crayons does she pack in total? Show your working using the break-apart strategy.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 19 into 10 + 9, multiply each part by 6, and add partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a partial-product table template with rows for '10 ×' and '9 ×'; stretch: ask what 29 × 6 equals using the same method.

exercise.description: Radha packs cupcakes in boxes of 4. She has packed 18 boxes. How many cupcakes? Use 10+8 decomposition.

items.prompt: A pond has 14 ducks and 9 frogs. Chippi the lizard counts all their legs. How many legs does Chippi see in total? (Ducks have 2 legs; frogs have 4 legs.)

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply legs per animal by number of animals for each type, then add the two products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw a table with two rows (ducks, frogs) and fill in legs per animal and total legs separately; stretch: add 6 beetles (6 legs each) and ask for the new total.

exercise.description: 25 geese and 12 sheep around a pond. Chippi the lizard sees many legs. How many legs does it see?

items.prompt: A factory has 76 tyres to build tricycles. Each tricycle needs 3 tyres. How many complete tricycles can be built? How many tyres are left over?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 25 tricycles with 1 tyre left over. 76 ÷ 3: take 10×3=30 (46 left), take 10×3=30 (16 left), take 5×3=15 (1 left); total 25 tricycles, remainder 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the partial quotient method: subtract convenient groups of 3 until fewer than 3 remain.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student the step-table scaffold with three rows to fill in; stretch: ask how many more tyres are needed to build one more tricycle.

exercise.description: Factory ordered 58 wheels for tempos, each with 3 wheels. How many tempos can be made? Discuss thinking at each step.

items.prompt: A sports shop has 62 shuttlecocks. They are packed in boxes of 4. How many full boxes can be packed? How many shuttlecocks are left over?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15 full boxes with 2 shuttlecocks left over. 62 ÷ 4: take 10×4=40 (22 left), take 5×4=20 (2 left); total 15 boxes, remainder 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract groups of 4 using convenient multiples (10×4 then 5×4) until fewer than 4 remain.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the step-table with 'groups taken', 'amount taken', and 'remaining' columns; stretch: ask how many shuttlecocks are needed to fill one more box completely.

exercise.description: Sports store packs 4 shuttlecocks in a box. They have 50 shuttlecocks. How many full boxes? How many are left?

items.prompt: A school has 136 students. Each student is given 5 colour pencils. How many colour pencils does the school need? Show your working using the break-apart strategy.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 136 into 100 + 30 + 6, multiply each part by 5, and add partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the three-row partial-product template; stretch: ask what the total would be if each student received 8 pencils.

exercise.description: 125 autorickshaws carry 8 passengers each. How many passengers total? Use 100+20+5 decomposition.

items.prompt: A ferry carries 9 people per trip. It needs to transport 117 people across a river. How many trips does the ferry need to make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 13 trips. 117 ÷ 9: take 5×9=45 (72 left), take 5×9=45 (27 left), take 3×9=27 (0 left); total 13 trips.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use partial quotient: subtract groups of 9 (5 nines at a time) until zero remains.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the step-table and start the first step; stretch: ask how many trips are needed for 162 people.

exercise.description: 9 boats ferry 108 people equally. How many people per boat? Use partial quotient method (5+5+2).

items.prompt: Meera saves ₹55 every month. (a) How much does she save in 4 months? (b) She shares her total savings equally among 4 friends. How much does each friend get?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply for part (a) using break-apart, then divide the product by 4 for part (b).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: solve part (a) using the partial-product table before attempting part (b); stretch: ask how much each friend gets if she saves for 6 months instead.

exercise.description: Anu saves ₹45 every month. (a) How much in 6 months? (b) Distribute total among 6 friends, how much each? (c) Distribute among 3 friends, how much each?

items.prompt: A truck carries 8 cartons per trip. A warehouse has 400 cartons to deliver. How many trips does the truck need to make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 50 trips. Basic fact: 4 ÷ 8 cannot simplify directly; use 40 ÷ 8 = 5, so 400 ÷ 8 = 50.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the basic fact 40 ÷ 8 = 5, then scale by ten: 400 ÷ 8 = 50.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write the pattern 8÷8, 80÷8, 800÷8 first then relate 400÷8 to 40÷8; stretch: ask how many trips for 480 cartons.

exercise.description: Solve: (1) 60 tyres ÷ 6 = how many trucks? (2) 80 wheels ÷ 4 = how many cars? (3) 600 ant legs ÷ 6 = how many ants? (4) 800 rubber bands ÷ 4 rubber bands per packet = how many packets?
